tour.title: Kota Tua: Batavia's Old Town
tour.summary: From company town to sinking megacity in two and a half kilometres — the old square, the canals, and the wooden sailing ships where this city began.
tour.overviewText:
Jakarta greets you with heat and noise, and then with the fact that almost nothing on the surface looks three hundred years old. The old town — Kota Tua, Indonesian for Old Town — is the exception: a pocket of Dutch gables and cobbles in the north of a city that has otherwise buried its past under towers.

This is where the modern city began. In 1619 the Dutch East India Company — the VOC, a private trading company with shareholders, its own ships and soldiers and a monopoly on Dutch trade in Asia — razed the port town of Jayakarta and built Batavia on the ruins. For two centuries this was the company's Asian headquarters, the warehouse and counting house through which pepper, nutmeg, cloves, coffee and sugar flowed to Europe. The Dutch dug canals to make the tropics look like Amsterdam, planted trees along them and called the place Koningin van het Oosten — Queen of the East. It did not work out as advertised: the canals stood still, bred malaria, and killed so many Europeans that Batavia earned a second nickname, the cemetery of Europeans. In October 1740, after sugar prices collapsed and unrest grew, the company turned on the city's Chinese population and killed at least ten thousand people in two weeks; the survivors were pushed outside the walls to Glodok, still Jakarta's Chinatown. In 1808 the colonial government abandoned the unhealthy old town and moved south to a district called Weltevreden. Kota Tua was left behind, which is the only reason its streets survived intact.

Two things make this walk more than nostalgia. First, the harbour at its end is older than the Dutch: Sunda Kelapa was the main port of the Sunda Kingdom for centuries before the Europeans arrived, and it still works, handling traditional wooden pinisi sailing ships. Second, the city around you is the future: a metropolitan region of roughly forty-two million people by the United Nations' 2025 count, with eleven million inside Jakarta's own borders, sinking in places by up to twenty-five centimetres a year, while the government builds a new capital, Nusantara, in the forests of Borneo. You are walking the opening chapters of a very long story.

The route is short and flat: about 2.5 kilometres and thirty-five minutes of walking, with museums to go into along the way. You start on the old town square, cross it to the former city hall, look at puppets and a colonial coffee house, then follow the old canal north to the harbour, ending on the quay where Jakarta began.

Practicalities: this is a hot, humid, equatorial city, so start early. The museums open around nine and mostly close by mid-afternoon, and many shut on Mondays. Carry water, a hat and small rupiah notes — the rupiah, Rp, runs at roughly sixteen thousand to the US dollar, so check the day's rate — because tickets are cheap but are sometimes sold on a prepaid card rather than in cash. Late afternoon works too, when the square fills with food carts and lights, but then the museums are closed. Grab or Gojek, the ride-hailing apps everyone here uses, will get you back.

Walk it slowly, drink something cold at the end, and remember: everything you see began as a gamble on spices.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. Flat, but hot and humid, with a cobbled square, uneven quays and one slightly humped wooden bridge. Museum interiors have entrance steps and stairs.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start early, around 7 to 8am: the air is cooler, the harbour is working, and the museums open at nine. Late afternoon is the alternative — golden light on the canal and a lively square — but the museums mostly close by 3pm and shut on Mondays.

stops.name: Taman Fatahillah
stops.narration:
Stand in the middle and turn slowly. This square — Taman Fatahillah, named for the sixteenth-century commander who took this port for Islam — was the centre of Batavia, the city the Dutch built here and ran for three centuries. Everything around you is a piece of that story: the old city hall on the south side, the church site on the west, the shophouses and warehouses on the north, the old court of justice to the east.

Start with who built it. In 1619 the Dutch East India Company — the VOC, Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie in Dutch, a private company chartered in 1602 with shareholders, ships, soldiers and a monopoly on Dutch trade in Asia — attacked and razed the port town of Jayakarta. On its ruins the company laid out Batavia, named after the Batavi, a Germanic tribe the Dutch believed were their ancestors. The square was first recorded around 1627 as the Nieuwe Markt, the New Market, and became the Stadhuisplein, the city hall square, once the government moved in.

Now look at what the Dutch tried to do here. They dug canals, lined them with coconut palms, built brick warehouses and step-gabled houses, and called the result Koningin van het Oosten — Queen of the East. It was a boast with a bill attached. The canals barely flowed in the equatorial heat; they bred mosquitoes and malaria, and Batavia became known across Europe as the cemetery of Europeans, a place where newly arrived Dutch officials often died in their first year. Meanwhile the city inside the walls was never Dutch: most residents were Chinese merchants and artisans, Mardijkers — free people of mixed Asian and European descent — Malays, and thousands of enslaved people from Bali, Sulawesi and India. Javanese were forbidden to live inside the walls. Their descendants, mixed across all of it, are the Betawi, the old creole people of Jakarta.

Two objects to find before you leave. In the middle stands a fountain that supplied the colonial city's water, and near it a Portuguese cannon called Si Jagur, with a hand carved on its breech making a rude gesture that locals long believed helped women conceive. And look at the paving: this square was cleared of traffic in 2007 and rebuilt in a big restoration finished in 2022, which is why it now belongs to food carts, rented bicycles and families rather than cars.

The square is free and open at all hours, and it is at its best in the late afternoon, when the lights come on and the carts start smoking. Cross it now to the big building on the south side.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free public square, open at all hours. Food carts, rented bicycles and the cafés around it charge their own prices.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Liveliest from late afternoon into the evening, when the food carts and lights arrive.
stops.accessibility: Level paved square, step-free across the cobbles. Watch for bicycles, carts and uneven stone.
stops.insiderTip: Find the Portuguese cannon Si Jagur and the hand carved on its breech — locals once believed the gesture helped women conceive. Late afternoon, when the carts fire up and the lights come on, is the square at its best.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk to the south side of the square, to the big building with the domed cupola and the wide flight of steps. That is the former city hall, the Jakarta History Museum — about eighty metres across the cobbles.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Uncredited, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Jakarta History Museum
stops.narration:
You are looking at the Stadhuis, the city hall of Batavia, and it was built to intimidate. The first version went up in the 1620s; the building in front of you was rebuilt between 1707 and 1710 and inaugurated by Governor-General Abraham van Riebeeck as the administrative headquarters of the Dutch East India Company. The model was the Paleis op de Dam in Amsterdam — domed cupola, classical proportions, massive timber floors — which is to say the Dutch reproduced their capital's town hall in the tropics and made it the seat of government for everything they held in Asia.

Walk in and read it as a machine for ruling. The council chamber, where the Governor-General and the Council of the Indies decided the affairs of a trading empire. The courtroom. The strongrooms. And under the front portico, low dark openings that served as the city's dungeons until 1846. One prisoner matters to every Indonesian schoolchild: Prince Diponegoro, the Javanese aristocrat who led the Java War against Dutch rule from 1825 to 1830, was held here in 1830 after being invited to negotiations and then arrested, before exile to Manado and Makassar. The Dutch never quite lived that betrayal down.

The museum opened in 1974 and holds around 23,500 objects: prehistoric finds, the Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms of western Java — look for the replica of the Tugu inscription, a fifth-century stone naming King Purnawarman of Tarumanagara — the VOC centuries, and the independence struggle of the 1940s. There is also a stone tablet set into a wall showing a VOC sailing ship, and a room of richly carved Betawi furniture. After the company went bankrupt in 1799, the building carried on as the colonial city hall until 1913, long after the government had moved south.

Practicalities: this is one of the few stops that charges. Indonesian adults pay around Rp10,000 on weekdays and Rp15,000 at weekends, students and children less, foreign visitors around Rp50,000 — all worth confirming at the gate, since rates move and tickets are sometimes sold on a prepaid JakCard rather than in cash. Hours are typically Tuesday to Sunday, roughly 09:00 to 15:00, closed Monday; verify on the day. There is a broad flight of steps to the entrance and stairs inside, so it is not step-free.

Buy your ticket, go in, and give it half an hour. Then come back out onto the square and turn right, to the smaller building on the western side.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Indonesian adults around Rp10,000 weekdays, Rp15,000 weekends; students and children less; foreign visitors around Rp50,000. Verify at the gate — rates move and tickets are sometimes sold on a prepaid JakCard rather than in cash.
stops.openingHours: Typically Tuesday to Sunday, roughly 09:00 to 15:00, closed Monday. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Not step-free: a broad flight of steps to the entrance, then stairs between floors and uneven old thresholds inside.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the cells beneath the front portico — the city's dungeons until 1846, where Prince Diponegoro was held in 1830. Inside, find the stone tablet showing a VOC ship set into the wall.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come back out onto the square and turn right, to the smaller white building on the western side with the tall windows. That is the Wayang Museum, about a hundred and twenty metres away.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Herusutimbul, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Wayang Museum
stops.narration:
This modest building hides the strangest history on the square, so take it in two layers. Under your feet was a Dutch church: built in 1640 as the Oude Hollandsche Kerk, rebuilt in 1732 as the Nieuwe Hollandsche Kerk, and destroyed by an earthquake in 1808. In its churchyard was buried Jan Pieterszoon Coen, the VOC governor-general who founded Batavia — the man who razed Jayakarta in 1619 and who, in 1621, had most of the population of the Banda Islands killed, enslaved or deported to secure the nutmeg monopoly. A warehouse went up on the site in 1912, and in 1975 it became the Wayang Museum.

Above that layer is the reason to come. Wayang is the traditional puppet theatre of Java, and it is not a children's show. The word covers the performance and the puppet; the stories come mostly from the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, the Hindu epics that reached Java from India well over a thousand years ago and were then rewritten with local heroes, local humour and local politics. Two forms dominate the collection here. Wayang kulit are flat puppets cut from buffalo hide and painted, worked behind a lit screen so the audience watches shadows. Wayang golek are three-dimensional wooden puppets on rods. Running the whole thing is the dalang, the puppeteer-narrator who voices every character, cues the gamelan — the bronze percussion orchestra seated behind him — and can keep a show going from midnight until dawn. It is one of the most demanding performance jobs on earth, and UNESCO lists wayang puppet theatre as intangible cultural heritage.

The cases hold puppets from across Indonesia and beyond, including Chinese hand puppets, and there are usually free guides on duty. Coen's tombstone plate is displayed inside — find it, because it ties the two layers together: the founder of the Dutch city lies under the floor of a museum of Javanese culture, in a building the Dutch built on a church the Dutch lost.

The fee is small: around Rp10,000 on weekdays and Rp15,000 at weekends for Indonesians, less for students, around Rp50,000 for foreign visitors — verify at the gate. Hours are typically Tuesday to Sunday, roughly 09:00 to 15:00, closed Monday. There are steps at the entrance and stairs to the upper floor. Twenty minutes is enough; a live performance, if you catch one, is not.

Leave and walk along the north side of the square to the green-roofed building with the shutters.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Around Rp10,000 weekdays and Rp15,000 weekends for Indonesians, less for students, around Rp50,000 for foreign visitors. Verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Typically Tuesday to Sunday, roughly 09:00 to 15:00, closed Monday. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Steps at the entrance and stairs to the upper floor; the ground-floor display rooms are cramped.
stops.insiderTip: Find Coen's tombstone plate inside, and ask whether a guide is free — they are usually on duty and will demonstrate how wayang kulit shadows are worked behind the screen.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the Wayang Museum and follow the north side of the square to the green-roofed building with the shutters and the terrace. That is Café Batavia, about eighty metres east.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Herusutimbul, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Café Batavia
stops.narration:
Sit down. This is the right place to rest your legs, because the building is itself a lesson. Parts of it go back to about 1805, which makes it the second-oldest structure on the square after the city hall you just visited, and it has been a trading house, a warehouse and a shop before becoming the café it is today. The walls are covered with photographs of old Batavia; the shutters and dark wood are the atmosphere the Dutch were imitating, and the air conditioning is the thing they never had.

While you drink, here is the story the pretty room is standing on. Batavia was a company town. The VOC appointed a governor-general and a council, fixed prices, ran the courts and defended the walls, and it did all of this with a population that was mostly not Dutch. Inside the walls lived Chinese merchants and craftsmen, Mardijkers — free people of mixed Asian and European descent — Malays, and a large enslaved population brought from Bali, Sulawesi, India and beyond; at times more than half the city's people were enslaved. Javanese were barred from living inside the walls. Dutch men took Asian wives and partners, and the mixed society that grew out of it became the Betawi, the creole people of Jakarta, whose language and food still mark the city.

Now the two disasters. The first was slow and biological: the canals the Dutch dug to look like Amsterdam did not flow, mosquitoes bred in them, and malaria and dysentery killed Europeans so reliably that Batavia was nicknamed the cemetery of Europeans. Wealthy families moved to the higher, healthier ground south of here, and in 1808 Governor-General Herman Willem Daendels moved the whole colonial administration out with them, to a district called Weltevreden. The old town was abandoned by the people who ran it, and that is the only reason its streets survived intact for you to walk today.

The second disaster was deliberate. By 1740 the city held roughly 10,000 Chinese residents, many of them sugar-mill workers, and when sugar prices fell and unrest grew, the government of Governor-General Adriaan Valckenier turned on them. Between 9 and 22 October 1740 Dutch troops and allied militia killed at least 10,000 ethnic Chinese — some historians say more — and burned their quarter. The survivors were moved outside the walls to a district called Glodok, which is still Jakarta's Chinatown, a few minutes' walk south of where you are sitting.

The café is free to look at; you pay menu prices to sit, and they are Jakarta restaurant prices, not street prices. It usually opens in the morning and runs late — check the board at the door. Upstairs window seats give the best view of the square if they are free.

When you are ready, leave by the north-west corner and head away from the square, down Jalan Pintu Besar, towards the canal.
stops.entranceFeeNote: No charge to walk in and look; you pay menu prices to sit, and they are Jakarta restaurant prices rather than street prices. Verify hours and the menu at the door.
stops.openingHours: Typically open from morning until late evening. Confirm at the door.
stops.accessibility: Step or two at the entrance; ground floor is manageable, but the upper floor and window seats are reached by stairs.
stops.insiderTip: Head upstairs for the window seats over the square if they are free — the walls are a photo archive of old Batavia, and the upstairs room is the best place on the square to sit out the midday heat.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave Café Batavia by the north-west corner and walk away from the square, down Jalan Pintu Besar, for about five hundred metres. Keep the canal on your right; the wooden drawbridge ahead of you is Kota Intan.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Hkurniawan (talk), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Kota Intan Drawbridge & Kali Besar
stops.narration:
This is the oldest bridge in Indonesia, and it is still doing its job. The Kota Intan bridge — the name means Diamond City — was built by the VOC in 1628, which makes it roughly four centuries old. It has been renamed so often that the names alone tell the history: first the Engelse Brug, the English Bridge, after the English trading post on the far bank; then the Hoenderpasarbrug, the Chicken Market Bridge, for the poultry market beside it; then the Central Bridge; and in the twentieth century the Queen Juliana Bridge, after a Dutch queen. After independence it took the name of the vanished Diamond bastion of Batavia Castle, which once stood at this end. It is a bascule bridge — a drawbridge — and its two wooden leaves used to swing up to let boats through, which is why it is built in that slight arc.

Now look along the water. This canal is the Kali Besar, the Great River, the straightened mouth of the Ciliwung, the 119-kilometre river that comes down from the mountains above Bogor. The Dutch straightened the bend here in 1631 and 1632, and for the next two centuries this was the artery of their trade. Ocean-going ships could not come this far up, so cargo was transferred to lighters and rowed in to the warehouses lining both banks. Behind these walls they stored and weighed pepper, nutmeg, cloves, coffee, sugar, indigo and textiles — the goods that made a small European country rich.

Read the buildings as a business district in layers. Back towards the square, on the west bank, stands Toko Merah, the Red Shop, built around 1730 for Gustaaf Willem van Imhoff, later a governor-general, then a naval academy, then a hotel with stables and carriages, and in 1851 bought by Oey Liauw Kong, the Dutch-appointed Kapitein der Chinezen — the captain of Batavia's Chinese community — who painted it the colour that gave it its name. William Bligh, the captain set adrift by the mutineers of the Bounty, was a guest there. Around 1900 the whole canal was rebuilt again as the office district of trading companies and banks, and after Indonesian independence those offices moved south, leaving the warehouses to decay and then, more recently, to be restored as cafés and studios.

There is no ticket and no gate — this is a public quay, open at all hours, and the best time is the hour before sunset, when the light comes down the canal and the old facades turn gold. The bridge is wooden and slightly humped, and the pavements along the canal are uneven, so watch your footing. For the famous photograph, stand back on the quay and shoot the bridge with the water behind it.

Keep walking north along the canal, past the fish market, towards the warehouses at the harbour.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free public quay and bridge, open at all hours. No ticket and no gate.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Best in the hour before sunset, when the light comes down the canal.
stops.accessibility: The bridge is wooden and slightly humped with a handrail; the canal-side pavements are uneven and broken in places. Not step-free in the strict sense.
stops.insiderTip: Shoot the bridge from back along the quay so the water shows behind it — and remember that the canal's finest old house, the red 1730 Toko Merah where Captain Bligh once stayed, is about five hundred metres back towards the square you came from.
stops.nextStopDirections: Cross the bridge and follow the canal north for about six hundred and fifty metres, past the fish market and the moored boats, until you reach the long white VOC warehouses on the left. That is the Maritime Museum.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Panina Manina, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Maritime Museum & Syahbandar Tower
stops.narration:
These long white warehouses are the reason the Dutch came. They are the Westzijdsche Pakhuizen, the warehouses of the west bank, built between 1652 and 1771 beside the mouth of the Ciliwung, and they now hold the Maritime Museum — Museum Bahari. Step inside and you are standing in the storage rooms of the spice trade. In these vaults the VOC weighed, graded, packed and protected pepper, nutmeg, mace, cloves, coffee and sugar before loading them for Europe, and locked away the tin, copper and textiles that paid for them.

The economics are worth spelling out, because they explain everything you have walked past today. Nutmeg and cloves grew in only one place on earth — the Maluku Islands, the Spice Islands of eastern Indonesia — and for a long time no European knew exactly where. A sack of nutmeg bought in the islands for a few coins could sell in Amsterdam for hundreds of times that. The VOC existed to capture that difference: it was granted a monopoly, it fought the Portuguese, the Spanish, the English and local sultans for the sea lanes, and it ran this port as a private profit machine for two hundred years. When the company finally went bankrupt in 1799, the Dutch state took over its debts, its forts and its colony — which is how a trading company's headquarters became the capital of the Dutch East Indies.

The museum tells that story with models of boats from across the archipelago, navigation instruments, charts, and a section on the pinisi, the wooden sailing ship you are about to see. Be aware that a fire in January 2018 destroyed much of the building and its collection; it has been restored and reopened since, but displays change, so check before you count on it. Hours are typically Tuesday to Sunday, roughly 09:00 to 15:00, closed Monday, with a small ticket of a few thousand rupiah for Indonesians and more for foreign visitors — confirm at the gate. The warehouses are old and uneven, with stairs and dark corners.

Beside the museum stands the Menara Syahbandar, the colonial harbormaster's lookout tower, built on the base of an older Dutch bastion. If it is open, pay the small fee and climb: from the top you get the whole thing at once — the river mouth, the quay, the masts, and the sea that carried all of it.

Then walk out towards the water and the masts.
stops.entranceFeeNote: A small ticket of a few thousand rupiah for Indonesians and more for foreign visitors; the tower may charge separately. Verify at the gate, and check the museum is open after its 2018 fire and restoration.
stops.openingHours: Typically Tuesday to Sunday, roughly 09:00 to 15:00, closed Monday. Confirm on the day, and confirm the museum is open after its 2018 fire and restoration.
stops.accessibility: Old warehouse floors, uneven thresholds, stairs and dark corners; not step-free. The tower climb is by steep stairs.
stops.insiderTip: If the Menara Syahbandar tower is open, pay the small fee and climb it — the view over the quay, the masts and the river mouth pulls the whole walk together in one glance.
stops.nextStopDirections: You cannot walk straight from here to the pinisi quay — the harbour basin is in the way. Walk back south past the museum, then follow the road round the eastern side of the basin (Jl. Lodan Raya, then Jl. Sunda Kelapa) for about a kilometre, roughly fifteen minutes, until you come out on the west quay at Jl. Maritim Raya where the masts are. That is Sunda Kelapa — the last stop. If that sounds like too much in the heat, a Grab or Gojek car will do the same trip in a few minutes.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: RaymondSutanto, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Sunda Kelapa Harbour
stops.narration:
You have arrived at the beginning. Everything you walked through today was built to serve this harbour, and the harbour was here long before the Dutch. Sunda Kelapa — the name means the coconut of Sunda — was the main port of the Sunda Kingdom, a Hindu kingdom of western Java, from roughly the thirteenth to the sixteenth century. Its capital, Pakuan Pajajaran, lay about sixty kilometres inland to the south, near modern Bogor, and the Ciliwung river connected the two. The trade was pepper, mostly, and it drew ships from China, India, the Malay peninsula and the Arabian Sea. In 1522 the Portuguese signed a treaty with the Sunda king for a share of it; five years later, in 1527, a commander named Fatahillah, sent by the Sultanate of Demak — the first Islamic state in Java — took the port from them and renamed it Jayakarta, the city of victory. That is the town the Dutch destroyed in 1619 to build Batavia, and that is why the square you started on is called Taman Fatahillah.

Now look at the water. The two-masted wooden ships tied up here are pinisi, the traditional sailing cargo vessels of the Bugis and Makassar seafarers of South Sulawesi, built by Konjo boatwrights in villages such as Ara and Tanaberu and still working this quay as a fleet of inter-island freighters. The rig — seven or eight sails on two masts — is a specific and clever piece of engineering, and the boatbuilding tradition behind it was added to UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2017. These are working ships, not museum pieces: crews load and unload cargo here, often timber and building materials, so ask before photographing anyone, and stay clear of the gangways and the swinging loads.

Notice too what happened to the Dutch here. Their ships grew too big and the estuary silted up, so in 1885 they opened a new deep-water port at Tanjung Priok, nine kilometres east, and abandoned this one to the small wooden boats. The old harbour survived precisely because it became unimportant.

That is the whole arc of this city in one view: a fourteenth-century pepper port, a seventeenth-century company town, and today a metropolitan region of some forty-two million people — one of the largest on earth — with eleven million inside Jakarta's own boundaries. It is also sinking. Parts of North Jakarta are subsiding by up to twenty-five centimetres a year as groundwater is pumped out from under the soft clay, and large areas of the north now sit below sea level. So the government is building a new capital, Nusantara, in the forests of East Kalimantan on Borneo, and relocating civil servants there from 2026; a Constitutional Court ruling in 2026 confirmed that Jakarta remains the capital for now while that move proceeds. Supporters call it a rescue; critics call it an escape from a problem that has not been solved, only left behind.
stops.entranceFeeNote: No entrance fee to walk the quays. Boat rides, guides and any small unofficial charges for specific areas are arranged privately — agree a price first.
stops.openingHours: Open daylight hours; it is a working port. Best in the early morning, when the crews are loading and unloading.
stops.accessibility: Level but rough quay surface, with gaps, mooring ropes, vehicles and swinging loads. Take real care, and do not step onto a ship uninvited.
stops.insiderTip: These are working cargo ships, not exhibits. Stand back, ask before photographing any crew member, and if a boatman offers a short harbour ride, agree the price and the length before you get in.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is the end of the walk, on the quay where Jakarta began. To get back, the old town square is about two kilometres south along the canal — roughly twenty-five to thirty minutes on foot, and hot work. Easier is a Grab or Gojek car, the ride-hailing apps everyone here uses, which will return you to the square or to Jakarta Kota station in about ten minutes. Or simply stay a while: watch a crew warp a wooden ship along the quay with ropes, buy something cold, and let the oldest part of the city do what it has done for six hundred years — take on cargo and send it somewhere else.
